content: West Nile virus (WNV) is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus that belongs to the family Flaviviridae and is classified within the Japanese encephalitis serocomplex. It was first isolated in Uganda in 1937 and has since spread globally. Birds serve as the primary natural reservoir for the virus, which is most commonly transmitted to humans and other animals through the bites of Culex mosquitoes. Human-to-human transmission is rare but can occur via blood transfusions or tissue transplantation. WNV infection presents as a clinical spectrum. It can be asymptomatic, manifest as a mild febrile illness known as West Nile fever, or progress to a severe neuroinvasive disease, which may include meningitis, encephalitis, or acute flaccid paralysis. While the infection often resolves spontaneously in immunocompetent individuals, it can lead to severe complications or death in elderly patients, immunosuppressed individuals, or those with comorbidities such as malignancies, advanced cardiovascular disease, or renal disease. Diagnosis of WNV infection is typically achieved through serological testing, such as IgM antibody assays, or molecular methods like reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Plaque reduction neutralization tests (PRNT) are used to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate WNV from other flavivirus infections. Immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry can also aid in identifying the virus in tissue samples. Management of WNV infection is primarily supportive, focusing on symptom relief and prevention of complications. Antiviral therapies, such as interferon-alpha-2b or ribavirin, have been used in severe neuroinvasive cases, although their efficacy remains under investigation. Universal screening for WNV is not recommended, but nucleic acid testing (NAT) is mandatory for blood and organ donors to prevent transmission. The prognosis for mild cases of WNV infection is excellent, but severe neuroinvasive disease can result in permanent neurological deficits or death. Risk factors for severe disease include advanced age, immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and renal disease. Environmental factors, such as warm temperatures and outdoor exposure, also increase the risk of mosquito-borne transmission. Preventive measures include community-level mosquito control programs, personal protective measures to reduce exposure to mosquito bites, and screening of blood and organ donors. Currently, there is no approved human vaccine for WNV, but vaccine candidates are under development and have shown promise in early clinical trials. Investigational therapies, including ribavirin and interferon-alpha-2b, are being studied for their potential to treat WNV central nervous system infections.
